basic_information.name: Agent Evaluation & Benchmarks
basic_information.creator: Aggregated from multiple academic institutions, companies, and organizations. Key benchmark creators: Princeton University (SWE-bench), Meta-FAIR / Hugging Face (GAIA), Tsinghua University THUDM (AgentBench), Carnegie Mellon / web-arena-x (WebArena, VisualWebArena), XLang Lab (OSWorld), Sierra Research (TAU-bench), OpenAI (MLE-bench), METR (HCAST), Scale AI (SWE-bench Pro), Writer (CUB), Galileo AI (Agent Leaderboard), Letta (Context-Bench), Anthropic (Bloom). Evaluation platform vendors: Braintrust, Langfuse, Arize, Maxim AI, Galileo AI.
basic_information.release_date: SWE-bench: October 2023 (ICLR 2024). GAIA: November 2023 (ICLR 2024). AgentBench: August 2023 (ICLR 2024). WebArena: July 2023 (NeurIPS 2024). OSWorld: April 2024 (NeurIPS 2024). TAU-bench: June 2024, TAU2-bench: June 2025. MLE-bench: October 2024 (ICLR 2025). SWE-bench Verified: August 2024 (OpenAI). SWE-bench Pro: 2025 (Scale AI). HCAST: 2024-2025 (METR). CUB: mid-2025 (Writer). WebArena Verified: January 2026. OSWorld-Verified: 2025. Context-Bench: October 2025 (Letta). Bloom: 2025 (Anthropic). Galileo Agent Leaderboard v2: January 2025.
basic_information.license: Mostly open-source: SWE-bench (MIT), AgentBench (open-source, THUDM GitHub), WebArena (open-source), OSWorld (open-source), MLE-bench (open-source, OpenAI GitHub), TAU-bench (open-source, Sierra Research GitHub), Multi-SWE-bench (Apache 2.0). GAIA dataset on Hugging Face. Some evaluation platforms are proprietary (Braintrust, Arize) or open-source (Langfuse). CUB and SWE-bench Pro are proprietary/managed by Scale AI and Writer respectively.
basic_information.current_version: SWE-bench: expanded to SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, SWE-bench Live, Multi-SWE-bench, SWE-bench Multimodal (January 2025). WebArena: expanded to WebArena Verified (January 2026), VisualWebArena, WebChoreArena. OSWorld: expanded to OSWorld-Verified, OSWorld-Human, OSWorld-MCP. TAU-bench: evolved to TAU2-bench (2025). METR HCAST: Time Horizon 1.1 (January 2026, 228 tasks). Galileo Agent Leaderboard: v2 (2025).

technical_architecture.architecture_pattern: N/A — this entry is market data covering the agent evaluation and benchmarking landscape, not a single technical product. The benchmarks evaluate agents across all architecture patterns: single_agent (SWE-bench, MLE-bench), multi_agent (AgentBench multi-agent scenarios), orchestrator (TAU-bench tool-agent-user), pipeline (WebArena multi-step workflows), and graph_based (GAIA multi-tool reasoning).
technical_architecture.underlying_models: Benchmarks are model-agnostic and evaluate all major LLMs. Current top performers by benchmark: SWE-bench Verified — Claude Opus 4.5 (79.2%), Gemini 3 Pro (77.4%). SWE-bench Pro — Claude Opus 4.5 (45.89%), Claude 4.5 Sonnet (43.60%), Gemini 3 Pro (43.30%), GPT-5 (41.78%). GAIA — H2O.ai h2oGPTe (65%), Google (49%), Microsoft (38%). WebArena — IBM CUGA (61.7%). OSWorld — recent agent (76.26%, superhuman vs 72% human baseline). Galileo Agent Leaderboard — GPT-4.1 (62% action completion). Models evaluated include GPT-4/GPT-4.1/GPT-5, Claude 3.5/3.7/Opus 4.5, Gemini 2.0/3 Pro, open-source models (Llama, Qwen, Mistral).
technical_architecture.tool_integration: Benchmarks test various tool integration methods. GAIA tests web browsing, code execution, multi-modal tool use. WebArena/VisualWebArena test browser-based interaction (clicking, typing, navigating). TAU-bench evaluates structured function calling with domain-specific APIs. OSWorld tests desktop GUI interaction (keyboard, mouse, screen reading). AgentBench tests 8 distinct environments including OS, database, web browsing. MLE-bench evaluates ML pipeline tool use (training, data processing, experimentation). CUB tests end-to-end workflows across business applications. Evaluation platforms (Braintrust, Langfuse, Arize) integrate via SDKs, OpenTelemetry, and framework-specific hooks (LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK).
technical_architecture.planning_approach: Benchmarks measure planning capabilities rather than implementing specific approaches. SWE-bench: tests ability to plan code changes across complex codebases. GAIA: tests multi-step reasoning and tool selection planning. WebArena: tests web navigation planning (goal decomposition into browser actions). OSWorld: tests desktop task planning across multiple applications. AgentBench: tests planning and decision-making in multi-turn open-ended settings. TAU-bench: tests policy-following and tool selection in constrained domains. METR HCAST: specifically measures autonomous planning over extended time horizons, finding steady exponential increases in models' human-equivalent time horizon.
technical_architecture.multi_agent_support: Some benchmarks explicitly test multi-agent scenarios. AgentBench: evaluates LLMs in multi-turn interactive settings across 8 environments. TAU2-bench: introduces dual-control where both agent and simulated user take actions. WebArena: primarily single-agent, but WebChoreArena introduces more complex multi-step scenarios. GAIA: single-agent but requires coordinating multiple tools. Multi-SWE-bench: tests multi-language issue resolution. Most evaluation platforms (Langfuse, LangSmith, Braintrust) support tracing multi-agent workflows with nested spans.

memory_and_context.memory_types_supported: N/A — market data entry. Benchmarks test various memory requirements: GAIA requires working memory across multi-step tasks. Context-Bench (Letta, October 2025) specifically evaluates long-running context management, testing whether agents can chain file operations, trace relationships, and make consistent decisions over extended multi-step workflows. OSWorld-Human evaluates efficiency of memory use (agents take 1.4-2.7x more steps than humans). METR HCAST measures autonomous task completion over extended time horizons requiring sustained memory.
memory_and_context.context_window_management: N/A — market data entry. Context management is an increasingly evaluated dimension. Context-Bench is the first benchmark specifically focused on context maintenance, reuse, and reasoning over long-running sessions. SWE-bench tasks require understanding large codebases (context window utilization is critical — Claude 3.7 Sonnet's 128K output tokens correlate with higher SWE-bench scores). METR Time Horizon measures how long agents can maintain effective context for autonomous work.
memory_and_context.persistence_mechanism: N/A — market data entry. Benchmarks use various persistence: SWE-bench uses Docker containers with git repositories. WebArena uses containerized web environments. OSWorld uses virtual machines (migrated from VMware/Docker to AWS in OSWorld-Verified with 50x parallelization). AgentBench provides 8 distinct persistent environments. Evaluation platforms persist data via cloud databases (Braintrust), self-hosted databases (Langfuse), or managed cloud (Arize).
memory_and_context.context_engineering_approach: Context engineering is emerging as a key evaluation dimension. Context-Bench (Letta, October 2025) treats context as a first-class evaluation concern, testing agents' ability to maintain and leverage context across extended interactions. The gap between benchmark performance and production deployment (the 'eval-deployment gap') is partly attributed to context management failures — models that dominate leaderboards often underperform when context conditions differ from benchmark setups. METR's Time Horizon methodology specifically measures how context engineering affects autonomous capability duration.

capabilities.core_capabilities: The agent evaluation and benchmarking landscape encompasses: (1) CODING BENCHMARKS: SWE-bench (resolving real GitHub issues, 2294 tasks), SWE-bench Verified (500 human-validated tasks), SWE-bench Pro (Scale AI, harder private subset), SWE-bench Live (continuously updated with fresh issues), Multi-SWE-bench (multilingual: Python, Go, JS, TS, Java, Rust), MLE-bench (75 Kaggle ML competitions). (2) WEB/BROWSER BENCHMARKS: WebArena (812 web tasks across e-commerce, forums, maps, GitLab), WebArena Verified (reproducible re-evaluation, 11.3pp less false negatives), VisualWebArena (910 multimodal web tasks), WebChoreArena (532 tedium-focused tasks), BearCubs (computer-using web agents). (3) DESKTOP/OS BENCHMARKS: OSWorld (369 real desktop tasks across Ubuntu/Windows/macOS), OSWorld-Verified (improved infrastructure on AWS), OSWorld-Human (human trajectory baselines), OSWorld-MCP (MCP tool evaluation), CUB (106 end-to-end business workflows across 7 industries). (4) GENERAL ASSISTANT BENCHMARKS: GAIA (450 questions testing reasoning + tool use at 3 difficulty levels), AgentBench (8 distinct interactive environments for LLM-as-agent evaluation). (5) TOOL USE BENCHMARKS: TAU-bench/TAU2-bench (tool-agent-user interaction in real-world domains like retail and telecom), Galileo Agent Leaderboard (tool selection quality + action completion across business domains). (6) SAFETY/AUTONOMY BENCHMARKS: METR HCAST (189 tasks for measuring autonomous capabilities of frontier models, human-calibrated), METR Time Horizon (measures exponential growth of autonomous capability duration). (7) SPECIALIZED: Context-Bench (long-running context management), Bloom (Anthropic, behavioral evaluations for alignment). (8) EVALUATION PLATFORMS: Galileo AI (agentic evaluations + observability), Braintrust (eval engineering + production guardrails), Langfuse (open-source LLM observability), Arize (drift detection + real-time alerting), Maxim AI (comprehensive testing). (9) EVALUATION FRAMEWORKS: CLEAR (Cost, Latency, Efficacy, Assurance, Reliability), CLASSic (Cost, Latency, Accuracy, Security, Stability), LLM-as-judge approaches.
capabilities.supported_modalities: N/A — market data entry. Benchmarks span all modalities: text (SWE-bench, AgentBench), code (SWE-bench, MLE-bench), vision/multimodal (VisualWebArena, OSWorld, SWE-bench Multimodal), browser (WebArena, CUB), desktop GUI (OSWorld), file system (SWE-bench, MLE-bench), voice (not yet a major benchmark dimension), structured APIs/function calling (TAU-bench, Galileo).
capabilities.autonomy_level: N/A — market data entry. Benchmarks measure a spectrum of autonomy: SWE-bench and MLE-bench require fully_autonomous operation (agent receives issue, must resolve independently). GAIA tests supervised multi-tool usage. WebArena and OSWorld test autonomous navigation with defined goals. METR HCAST specifically calibrates autonomous capability — measuring how long an agent can work without human intervention (time horizon). CUB tests end-to-end autonomous business workflow execution (highest score is only 10.4%, showing current limits of full autonomy).
capabilities.tool_ecosystem: N/A — market data entry. The benchmark ecosystem includes 50+ distinct benchmarks (per the ai-agent-benchmark-compendium GitHub repository by Philipp Schmid). Categories: Function Calling & Tool Use, General Assistant & Reasoning, Coding & Software Engineering, Computer Interaction. Evaluation platforms integrate with all major agent frameworks: LangChain/LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, AutoGen, LlamaIndex, Amazon Strands (Galileo supports all of these). Over 80 AI coding agents tracked on SWE-bench leaderboards.

agent_interoperability.mcp_support: OSWorld-MCP is specifically designed to benchmark MCP tool invocation capabilities alongside GUI operations. Evaluation platforms increasingly support MCP: Langfuse and Braintrust can trace MCP-mediated tool calls. The benchmark ecosystem itself does not mandate MCP, but agents evaluated on benchmarks increasingly use MCP for tool integration.
agent_interoperability.a2a_support: No current benchmarks specifically evaluate A2A (Agent-to-Agent Protocol) compliance or inter-agent communication. TAU2-bench's dual-control environment is the closest — testing how an agent interacts with a simulated user who can also take actions and call tools — but does not implement A2A protocol specifically. This is a gap in the current benchmark landscape.
agent_interoperability.agents_md_support: No current benchmarks specifically test AGENTS.md compliance. SWE-bench evaluates agents working in real GitHub repositories, some of which may contain project instruction files, but this is not a scored dimension.
agent_interoperability.cross_framework_compatibility: Evaluation platforms are increasingly framework-agnostic. Galileo integrates with CrewAI, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, LlamaIndex, and Amazon Strands. Langfuse provides open-source observability across frameworks. Braintrust supports any framework via its SDK. Benchmarks themselves are generally framework-agnostic — they evaluate agent output and task completion regardless of the underlying framework. The ai-agent-benchmark-compendium (Philipp Schmid) catalogs 50+ benchmarks in a unified taxonomy.

safety_and_guardrails.permission_model: N/A — market data entry. Safety benchmarks are a growing sub-category. METR specifically evaluates frontier model safety by testing autonomous capabilities and detecting reward hacking (where AI systems exploit bugs in scoring code or subvert task setup). METR observed that some systems demonstrate awareness that their behavior is not aligned with user intentions. Bloom (Anthropic) evaluates behavioral alignment by quantifying frequency and severity of undesired behaviors across automatically generated scenarios.
safety_and_guardrails.escalation_policy: N/A — market data entry. Current benchmarks primarily measure task completion and do not systematically evaluate escalation behavior. TAU-bench/TAU2-bench evaluates policy compliance — whether agents follow guidelines about when to escalate — but this is domain-specific (retail, telecom). The CLASSic framework includes 'Assurance' as a dimension covering appropriate escalation and safety guarantees.
safety_and_guardrails.hallucination_mitigation: A key evaluation dimension. GAIA specifically tests grounded reasoning — agents must produce verifiable, correct answers using real-world tools. SWE-bench measures whether code changes actually resolve the issue (functional verification, not just plausible-looking code). WebArena Verified was created to reduce false negatives (11.3pp improvement) — effectively mitigating the benchmark itself from 'hallucinating' success. The eval-deployment gap research shows models that appear reliable on benchmarks can fail dramatically on out-of-distribution inputs.
safety_and_guardrails.audit_trail: Evaluation platforms provide comprehensive audit trails. Langfuse offers open-source tracing with nested spans for multi-agent workflows. Braintrust provides eval engineering traces that bridge offline evaluation to production monitoring. Arize provides continuous performance monitoring with drift detection. Galileo's agentic evaluations produce detailed execution traces. All major benchmarks publish reproducible evaluation scripts (SWE-bench, WebArena, OSWorld).
safety_and_guardrails.human_oversight_pattern: METR HCAST uses human-calibrated baselines: 140 skilled people made 563 attempts across 189 tasks to establish human performance benchmarks. OSWorld-Human provides human trajectories as baselines. GAIA has human performance of 92% as the ceiling vs. AI at 15-65%. SWE-bench Verified uses human validation (OpenAI) to ensure tasks are correctly solvable. The broader trend is toward human-calibrated evaluation — ensuring benchmarks remain grounded in real human capability baselines.

governance_and_standards.governance_body: No single governance body for agent benchmarks. Key organizations: METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) — conducts safety evaluations for Anthropic and OpenAI. UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) publishes Frontier AI Trends Reports. Partnership on AI and IEEE are developing evaluation standards. World Economic Forum published 'AI Agents in Action: Foundations for Evaluation and Governance' (2025). Scale AI manages SWE-bench Pro as a commercial benchmark. NeurIPS, ICLR, and ICML serve as peer-review venues for benchmark papers. Hugging Face hosts leaderboards and datasets for GAIA, Bloom, and others.
governance_and_standards.contributing_protocols: Benchmarks contribute to evaluation standardization: SWE-bench established the paradigm of using real GitHub issues for code agent evaluation. GAIA established the paradigm of multi-tool reasoning with verifiable answers. WebArena pioneered containerized web environments for reproducible browser agent testing. METR's Time Horizon methodology provides a standardized way to measure autonomous capability growth. The CLEAR and CLASSic frameworks provide structured multi-dimensional evaluation protocols. LiveBench introduced contamination-resistant evaluation through monthly question refresh.
governance_and_standards.regulatory_compliance: EU_AI_Act is the primary regulatory driver for agent evaluation. Key requirements effective August 2025 for GPAI models: technical documentation for traceability, transparency reports on capabilities and limitations, structured evaluation and testing for 'systemic' models. High-risk AI systems (August 2026): conformity assessments, risk management, data governance, human oversight, accuracy/robustness testing, CE marking requirement. METR's work on autonomous capability measurement directly informs frontier AI safety policies — their December 2025 report documents 'Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies.' No specific regulatory standard yet for agent benchmarks themselves, but evaluation rigor is implicitly mandated by the EU AI Act's conformity assessment requirements.

deployment_and_operations.deployment_modes: Benchmarks: cloud (WebArena Verified on AWS, OSWorld-Verified on AWS with 50x parallelization), local (SWE-bench Docker containers, OSWorld VMware), hybrid. Evaluation platforms: cloud/managed_service (Braintrust, Arize, Galileo), local/self-hosted (Langfuse open-source), hybrid. WebArena Verified is available on PyPI (pip install webarena-verified) as of January 2026. Most benchmarks can be run locally with appropriate compute resources.
deployment_and_operations.scalability_model: Benchmark infrastructure is scaling rapidly. OSWorld-Verified migrated from VMware/Docker to AWS with 50x parallelization for faster evaluation runs. SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks) provides a faster subset when full evaluation is too expensive. Evaluation platforms use horizontal scaling: Braintrust and Arize are cloud-native with auto-scaling. Langfuse supports self-hosted deployments with configurable scaling. The Galileo Agent Leaderboard uses synthetic dataset generation to scale evaluation scenarios.
deployment_and_operations.cost_per_task: Benchmark evaluation costs vary widely. Per-sample evaluation with LLM-as-judge: $0.01-$0.10 per sample using GPT-4 class models. Specialized eval models (Galileo Luna-2): ~$0.0002 per million tokens (97% cheaper than GPT-4). Per-session agent costs on Galileo leaderboard: GPT-4.1 leads at 62% completion but at higher cost; GPT-4.1-mini offers ~5x lower cost with competitive performance. Running full SWE-bench (2294 tasks) with frontier models can cost hundreds of dollars in API fees. Running OSWorld requires VM infrastructure (now AWS-based). Evaluation platform pricing: Langfuse is free (open-source self-hosted), Braintrust offers free tier, Arize raised $70M Series C (February 2025) suggesting significant investment in enterprise pricing. Galileo announced free agent reliability platform (July 2025).
deployment_and_operations.resource_requirements: Benchmark infrastructure requirements: SWE-bench requires Docker for containerized execution, sufficient storage for repository clones, and LLM API access. WebArena/WebArena Verified requires containerized web servers (shopping, forum, CMS, GitLab instances). OSWorld requires VM infrastructure (Ubuntu, Windows, or macOS VMs) — OSWorld-Verified moved to AWS for scalability. METR HCAST requires isolated environments for safety evaluation of frontier models. MLE-bench requires GPU compute for ML training tasks. Evaluation platforms: Langfuse self-hosted requires PostgreSQL database and application server. Cloud platforms (Braintrust, Arize, Galileo) require only API integration.

observability_and_ops.monitoring_integration: The evaluation platform market is rapidly maturing. Key platforms with monitoring capabilities: Braintrust (used by Notion, Stripe, Zapier — bridges offline evals to production guardrails), Langfuse (open-source, deep integration with LangChain/LangGraph/CrewAI/OpenAI), Arize ($70M Series C, February 2025 — continuous monitoring, drift detection, real-time alerting), Maxim AI (comprehensive testing and monitoring), Galileo AI (agentic evaluations + free reliability platform announced July 2025). Emerging trend: organizations use combinations — e.g., Langfuse or Helicone for raw data logging, plus Braintrust or Maxim for advanced evaluation. All platforms support OpenTelemetry-compatible tracing.
observability_and_ops.tracing_support: Comprehensive tracing support across the evaluation ecosystem. Langfuse provides open-source nested span tracing for multi-agent workflows. Braintrust offers eval-to-production tracing continuity. Arize provides ML-native observability with LLM-specific traces. Galileo supports tracing across CrewAI, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, LlamaIndex, and Amazon Strands. Key 2025 trend: deeper agent tracing with support for multi-step agent workflows, nested tool calls, and sub-agent execution traces.
observability_and_ops.production_readiness_level: The benchmark ecosystem ranges from production_ready to experimental. Production-ready: SWE-bench (MIT licensed, widely adopted as industry standard), WebArena Verified (PyPI package, January 2026), GAIA (established leaderboard on Hugging Face). Beta/maturing: OSWorld-Verified (improved infrastructure but still evolving), TAU2-bench (new iteration with expanded domains), Context-Bench (newly released October 2025). Experimental: CUB (highest score only 10.4%), OSWorld-MCP (new MCP-specific evaluation). Evaluation platforms: Braintrust and Arize are enterprise_grade. Langfuse is production_ready. Galileo is production_ready with free tier.

adoption_and_market.github_stars: SWE-bench: ~3.8k stars (main repo). SWE-agent: major open-source project (NeurIPS 2024). AgentBench (THUDM): available on GitHub (ICLR 2024). WebArena: available on GitHub with verified version on PyPI. OSWorld: available on GitHub (NeurIPS 2024). MLE-bench: OpenAI official repo on GitHub. TAU-bench/TAU2-bench: Sierra Research GitHub repos. ai-agent-benchmark-compendium (Philipp Schmid): catalogs 50+ benchmarks. ai-agent-benchmark (murataslan1): tracks 80+ coding agents. The broader evaluation platform ecosystem has significant adoption: Langfuse is a top open-source LLM observability platform.
adoption_and_market.adoption_scale: SWE-bench has become the de facto standard for coding agent evaluation — cited in virtually every frontier model release (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta). Over 80 AI coding agents have submitted to SWE-bench leaderboards. GAIA leaderboard hosted at Princeton (hal.cs.princeton.edu/gaia) and Hugging Face. WebArena and OSWorld are standard academic benchmarks presented at top venues (NeurIPS, ICLR). METR conducts official safety evaluations for Anthropic, OpenAI, and the UK AISI. Galileo Agent Leaderboard hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. The benchmark ecosystem is seeing first benchmark-driven competition similar to how ImageNet spurred vision model progress a decade ago. Evaluation platform adoption: Braintrust used by Notion, Stripe, Zapier. Arize raised $70M Series C (February 2025). Galileo launched free platform (July 2025).
adoption_and_market.pricing_model: Benchmarks: predominantly open-source and free. SWE-bench (MIT, free), GAIA (free dataset on Hugging Face), AgentBench (free), WebArena (free, pip installable), OSWorld (free), MLE-bench (free, OpenAI GitHub), TAU-bench (free). SWE-bench Pro is managed by Scale AI (likely commercial for certified evaluations). Evaluation platforms: Langfuse (free open-source self-hosted, managed cloud plans), Braintrust (free tier + enterprise), Arize (enterprise pricing), Galileo (free reliability platform announced July 2025 + enterprise), Maxim AI (tiered pricing).
adoption_and_market.key_use_cases: Primary use cases for agent benchmarks and evaluation: (1) MODEL SELECTION: Companies use benchmark results to choose LLMs for agent deployments (SWE-bench for coding agents, GAIA for general assistants). (2) AGENT DEVELOPMENT: Benchmark-driven development — teams iterate on agent architectures targeting specific benchmark scores. (3) FRONTIER MODEL RACING: Labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) compete on SWE-bench, GAIA, OSWorld leaderboards as proof of model capability. (4) SAFETY EVALUATION: METR evaluations inform deployment decisions for frontier models and feed into safety policies. (5) PRODUCTION MONITORING: Evaluation platforms (Braintrust, Langfuse, Arize) monitor deployed agents for regression, drift, and failures. (6) ENTERPRISE PROCUREMENT: Companies use benchmark data to evaluate AI vendors and justify investment decisions. (7) REGULATORY COMPLIANCE: EU AI Act conformity assessments will require documented evaluation methodologies. (8) ACADEMIC RESEARCH: Benchmarks drive research in planning, reasoning, tool use, and multi-modal agent capabilities.
adoption_and_market.competitive_position: SWE-bench is the undisputed leader for coding agent evaluation — every major model release references it. GAIA is the leading general assistant benchmark. WebArena leads browser agent evaluation. OSWorld leads desktop/OS agent evaluation. MLE-bench is the standard for ML engineering agents. METR HCAST is the standard for safety-focused autonomous capability measurement. TAU-bench leads tool-agent-user interaction evaluation. CUB is emerging for business workflow evaluation but is still very early (10.4% max score). In the evaluation platform space: Langfuse leads open-source, Braintrust/Arize/Galileo compete for enterprise. The landscape is fragmented — no single benchmark covers all agent capabilities, requiring multi-benchmark evaluation strategies.

ecosystem_maturity.community_size: The agent evaluation community spans academic and industry. SWE-bench has an active ecosystem with 80+ agent submissions. GAIA has 5000+ leaderboard submissions on Hugging Face. WebArena has spawned multiple variants (Verified, Visual, Chore). OSWorld has an active research community (NeurIPS 2024, ICML 2025 presentations). METR works closely with frontier labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, UK AISI). Evaluation platform communities: Langfuse has a growing open-source community (GitHub + Discord). Braintrust, Arize, and Galileo have enterprise user bases. The AI agent benchmark compendium tracks 50+ benchmarks, indicating a vibrant ecosystem.
ecosystem_maturity.documentation_quality: good — Major benchmarks have published papers at top venues (ICLR, NeurIPS, ICML) with detailed methodology documentation. SWE-bench has comprehensive documentation on swebench.com. WebArena Verified includes improved documentation and PyPI packaging. OSWorld has detailed setup instructions. Evaluation platforms vary: Braintrust and Arize have excellent enterprise documentation. Langfuse has good open-source documentation. The field evolves rapidly, so documentation can lag behind latest developments.
ecosystem_maturity.third_party_integrations_count: 50+ benchmarks cataloged in the agent benchmark compendium. Evaluation platforms have broad integrations: Galileo supports CrewAI, LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, LlamaIndex, Amazon Strands. Langfuse integrates with all major agent frameworks. Braintrust provides universal SDK integration. The benchmark ecosystem integrates with Docker, AWS, PyPI, Hugging Face, and major LLM APIs.
ecosystem_maturity.tutorial_availability: Moderate to good. SWE-bench has official documentation, viewer tools, and community tutorials. WebArena and OSWorld have setup guides and research paper tutorials. GAIA has Towards Data Science articles and Hugging Face documentation. Evaluation platforms offer comprehensive tutorials: Braintrust (articles and guides), Arize (documentation and blog), Galileo (HuggingFace Space demo), Langfuse (self-hosting guides). Academic papers serve as primary tutorials for benchmark methodology. Evidently AI and o-mega.ai publish comprehensive benchmark guides.

human_agent_interaction.autonomy_spectrum: Benchmarks measure autonomy on a spectrum: SWE-bench/MLE-bench test fully_autonomous operation (agent works independently to resolve issues). GAIA tests autonomous multi-tool reasoning with defined goals. WebArena/OSWorld test autonomous computer use. CUB tests autonomous business workflow execution (current best: 10.4%). TAU2-bench tests a novel dual-control paradigm where both agent and user can act. METR Time Horizon specifically measures how long agents can operate autonomously — finding steady exponential growth in capability duration across model generations.
human_agent_interaction.handoff_mechanism: Not a primary focus of most benchmarks. TAU-bench/TAU2-bench is the closest — evaluating how agents interact with users, follow policies, and handle ambiguous requests in customer service scenarios. METR evaluates whether agents appropriately recognize their limitations. In production evaluation platforms (Braintrust, Langfuse), handoff behavior is monitored through tracing — detecting when agents fail and need human intervention. The CLASSic and CLEAR frameworks include dimensions for measuring appropriate human handoff behavior.
human_agent_interaction.feedback_loop: Benchmarks themselves provide feedback to the agent development ecosystem through leaderboard competition — benchmark results drive research investment and model improvement. SWE-bench Live provides continuously fresh tasks to prevent overfitting. LiveBench refreshes monthly to avoid contamination. OSWorld-Human provides human trajectory data as feedback for improving agent efficiency (agents take 1.4-2.7x more steps than necessary). Evaluation platforms implement production feedback loops: Braintrust bridges offline eval results to production guardrails, Arize provides real-time drift alerting, Langfuse enables manual annotation of traces for fine-tuning data.

entrepreneurial_relevance.startup_applicability: CRITICAL for startup founders building or deploying AI agents. Key insights: (1) BENCHMARK LITERACY: Understanding agent benchmarks is essential for making informed build-vs-buy decisions. SWE-bench scores directly predict coding agent capability; GAIA predicts general assistant quality; CUB predicts business workflow automation potential. (2) REALITY CHECK: The gap between benchmark and production performance is well-documented — models dominating leaderboards often underperform in deployment. The eval-deployment gap means startups cannot rely solely on benchmark numbers. (3) EVALUATION AS PRODUCT: The agent evaluation market is a significant opportunity itself — Arize raised $70M (Feb 2025), Galileo launched free platform (Jul 2025), Braintrust is used by Notion/Stripe/Zapier. Startups can build evaluation tools targeting specific verticals or agent types. (4) COST-EFFECTIVE EVAL: Open-source tools (Langfuse, SWE-bench, WebArena) enable startups to evaluate agents without expensive commercial platforms. Specialized eval models (Galileo Luna-2) cost 97% less than GPT-4 for evaluation. (5) BENCHMARK-DRIVEN DEVELOPMENT: Use benchmarks to validate your agent's capabilities before going to market. SWE-bench submission demonstrates coding agent competence. CUB submission demonstrates business workflow capability. (6) CONTAMINATION RISK: Be aware that static benchmarks can be gamed — prefer dynamic benchmarks (SWE-bench Live, LiveBench) for honest capability assessment. (7) COMPLIANCE PREPARATION: EU AI Act conformity assessments (August 2026) will require documented evaluation — building robust eval pipelines now creates regulatory readiness.
entrepreneurial_relevance.build_vs_buy: For startups needing agent evaluation: BUILD custom evaluation suites using open-source benchmarks (SWE-bench MIT, WebArena open-source, TAU-bench open-source) as foundations — adapt to your specific use case. BUY/USE evaluation platforms for production monitoring — Langfuse (free open-source) for budget-conscious startups, Galileo (free tier available) for comprehensive agentic evaluation, Braintrust or Arize for enterprise-grade needs. BUILD domain-specific benchmarks tailored to your vertical — generic benchmarks miss domain nuances. BUY benchmark infrastructure (AWS, Docker) rather than building from scratch. For agent selection: USE benchmark results as one input but always conduct domain-specific testing. The 40% agentic AI project failure rate (Gartner) correlates with inadequate evaluation — investing in evaluation infrastructure early saves significant costs. Cost: LLM-as-judge evaluation runs $0.01-$0.10/sample with GPT-4; specialized eval models bring this to $0.0002/million tokens.
entrepreneurial_relevance.session_mapping: Session 1 (AI landscape & benchmarking context), Session 3 (AI project management — evaluation as part of project lifecycle), Session 5 (Ethics & governance — benchmark limitations, EU AI Act conformity assessments, safety evaluation via METR). Benchmark data supports Session 1 by illustrating where AI capabilities truly stand vs. hype. Evaluation methodology is central to Session 3 project management. confidence.data_quality: Medium-High — Benchmark data comes from peer-reviewed academic papers (ICLR, NeurIPS, ICML), official leaderboards maintained by benchmark creators, and reputable evaluation platform vendors. Performance numbers on leaderboards are publicly verifiable. Market data for evaluation platforms comes from press releases, VC announcements, and vendor documentation. Some performance numbers are self-reported by model creators and may be subject to selection bias.

confidence.caveats: CRITICAL CAVEATS: (1) BENCHMARK SATURATION: Static benchmarks age quickly and become saturated — SuperGLUE was rapidly saturated, and similar dynamics are emerging for some SWE-bench subsets. Benchmark creators respond with harder variants (Pro, Live, Verified), creating a proliferation of benchmark versions. (2) DATA CONTAMINATION: Public benchmarks risk training data contamination — models may inadvertently train on test data. SWE-bench Pro and SWE-bench Live attempt to address this with private/fresh tasks. (3) EVAL-DEPLOYMENT GAP: Benchmark performance does not equal production performance. Models scoring highly on leaderboards often fail on out-of-distribution inputs. Distribution shift, spurious shortcuts, and Goodhart's law (optimizing the metric rather than the mission) contribute to this gap. (4) SELF-REPORTED SCORES: Some leaderboard submissions are self-reported by model creators, introducing potential selection bias. SWE-bench Verified and WebArena Verified attempt to address this with independent evaluation. (5) COST TRANSPARENCY: Running full benchmark suites is expensive (hundreds of dollars in API fees) but costs are rarely reported alongside performance numbers. (6) RAPIDLY EVOLVING: New benchmarks launch monthly. This data reflects the landscape as of early February 2026 and will need frequent updating. (7) BENCHMARK COMPETITION DYNAMICS: The benchmark-driven competition creates incentives for benchmark-specific optimization rather than general capability improvement.
